newsitem.title: UK: Patten says HK vote procedure "stomach churning".
newsitem.headline: Patten says HK vote procedure "stomach churning".

text.p: Hong Kong governor Chris Patten on Saturday described China's selection of a new Hong Kong lawmaking body as "stomach-churning" and said a tennis club would run its affairs better.

Speaking on BBC radio as China defied British objections and elected a provisional legislature with pro-Beijing politicians, Patten said the move will "throw question marks over the early months of the government of Hong Kong after July."
"What it shows about China is that here it is taking over responsibility for a First World economy but they're trying to foist on us political institutions which a Third World country would reject.
"Here we are having foisted on us institutions which, frankly, you wouldn't try to run a tennis club with," Patten said.
China has been bent on dismantling the current elected legislature after reforms brought in by Patten enlarged the democratic franchise before the handover of the territory in 1997.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind has already challenged China to go to the International Court of Justice in The Hague, which arbitrates treaty disputes, to get a ruling on the new body's legality.
The Foreign Office said on Saturday Britain had little to add to Rifkind's remarks.

In an interview published in Saturday's Independent newspaper, Patten said the procedure under which a carefully-screened elite of 400 Hong Kong electors voted to appoint 60 legislators was "stomach-churning."
"Here we have members of this appointed echo-chamber nominating one another, choosing one another, voting for one another," he said.
